title: Slow-cooker beef and barley stew
subtitle: A thick, filling stew that looks after itself all day
excerpt: Braising steak and pearl barley cooked low and slow with carrots, celery, and beef stock. The barley thickens the broth naturally and adds a nutty bite.
sourceNotes: Beef and barley stew is a staple of British and Scottish home cooking, appearing in versions throughout 19th and 20th century cookbooks including Florence White, Good Things in England (1932). Pearl barley as a thickening grain in slow-cooked stews is documented across many sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. The barley absorbs more liquid on reheating; add a splash of water or stock when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: This recipe scales well. Make a large batch on a weekend and portion for the week.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for up to 4 days. Reheat gently on the hob.

glossaryTerms.definition: Barley with its outer husk and bran removed, leaving a pale, rounded grain that cooks in around 30 to 40 minutes and thickens soups and stews as it absorbs liquid.

content.text: Beef and barley stew is one of the most self-sufficient things the slow cooker can do. Load it in the morning, come back in the evening to a pot of thick, dark broth with beef that pulls apart easily and
that has absorbed the cooking liquid and turned soft and nutty.

The barley does two things: it eats well as a grain, and it thickens the broth without any added flour. By the end of cooking, the liquid has a natural body that coats the spoon. This is a recipe that serves six people from one pot with minimal cost.
No sides needed. Crusty bread alongside is the only addition worth making.

Season {{braising-steak}} of braising steak generously with salt. Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil in a frying pan over high heat. Brown the beef in two batches, 2 to 3 minutes per side, until coloured. Transfer to the slow cooker.

Add {{onion}} diced onion, {{carrot}} carrot pieces, {{celery}} celery pieces, and {{garlic}} of crushed garlic to the slow cooker. Add the rinsed {{pearl-barley}} of pearl barley. Stir in {{tomato-puree}} of tomato puree and {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce. Pour over {{stock-beef}} of beef stock. Tuck in {{thyme}} of thyme and {{bay-leaves}} of bay.

Set the slow cooker to LOW and cook for 7 to 8 hours. The barley will have swelled and softened, the beef will pull apart easily, and the broth will have thickened. Discard the thyme stalks and bay leaves. Taste and adjust seasoning before serving.

rows.symptom: The stew is too thick and the barley has absorbed all the liquid
rows.cause: Pearl barley absorbs a large volume of liquid as it cooks. On the HIGH setting or with a smaller slow cooker, this can happen faster than expected.
rows.fix: Stir in 200 to 300 ml of boiling water or stock to loosen the stew. Taste and re-season.

rows.symptom: The beef is still tough after 8 hours
rows.cause: The low setting on some older slow cookers may not reach a temperature high enough to break down the connective tissue in braising steak.
rows.fix: Switch to HIGH for a further hour. This cut benefits from extended cooking time.

rows.cause: The broth was not seasoned well enough before cooking, or the stock was low-salt.
rows.fix: Stir in a teaspoon more Worcestershire sauce and re-season with salt. A splash of soy sauce also adds depth without adding a distinct flavour.

rows.symptom: The barley is still hard in the centre
rows.cause: The slow cooker may not have maintained a hot enough temperature throughout cooking.
rows.fix: Cook for a further hour on HIGH. Rinsing the barley before adding it helps it cook more evenly.

content.text: Barley has been thickening British stews since long before flour became universal. It appears in Scotch broth, in lamb stews, in the mutton soups of thrifty Victorian households. The combination with beef is a natural extension: inexpensive cut, cheap grain, long slow heat. This version belongs to the same tradition but asks very little of the cook.
